1.title: English Foundations
1.description: Grammar basics, sentence structure, and vocabulary building

chunks.content:
Words are classified by their function in a sentence.

The 8 Parts of Speech:
1. Noun: Names a person, place, thing, or idea
   Examples: dog, London, happiness, freedom

2. Pronoun: Replaces a noun
   Examples: he, she, it, they, we, I, you

3. Verb: Shows action or state of being
   Examples: run, think, is, were, become

4. Adjective: Describes a noun
   Examples: tall, beautiful, three, ancient

5. Adverb: Modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb
   Examples: quickly, very, often, loudly

6. Preposition: Shows relationship between words
   Examples: in, on, at, under, beside, through

7. Conjunction: Connects words, phrases, or clauses
   FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So

8. Interjection: Expresses sudden feeling
   Examples: Wow! Oh! Ouch!

A sentence must have a subject and a predicate.

Sentence Types by Structure:
• Simple: One independent clause
  'The dog barked.'

• Compound: Two independent clauses joined by a conjunction or semicolon
  'The dog barked, and the cat ran away.'

• Complex: One independent + one dependent clause
  'Although it was raining, she went for a walk.'

• Compound-Complex: Two independent + at least one dependent clause

Sentence Types by Purpose:
• Declarative: Makes a statement (ends with .)
• Interrogative: Asks a question (ends with ?)
• Imperative: Gives a command
• Exclamatory: Shows strong feeling (ends with !)

Common Errors to Avoid:
• Sentence Fragment: Incomplete thought ('Running to the store.')
• Run-on: Two sentences without proper punctuation

A rich vocabulary makes writing and communication more precise.

Word Formation Strategies:

Prefixes (beginnings that change meaning):
• un- (not): unhappy, unclear
• re- (again): rewrite, redo
• pre- (before): preview, prepare
• mis- (wrongly): misunderstand, mistake
• dis- (opposite): disagree, dishonest

Suffixes (endings that change function):
• -tion/-tion (noun): education, creation
• -ful (adjective): beautiful, careful
• -ly (adverb): quickly, softly
• -less (without): careless, hopeless

Context Clues: Use surrounding words to guess unfamiliar words.
'The boy was so loquacious that he never stopped talking.' → loquacious means talkative.

Synonyms (similar): happy / joyful / elated / glad
Antonyms (opposite): hot / cold, fast / slow

2.title: Intermediate English
2.description: Essay writing, literary devices, and advanced grammar

chunks.content:
A well-structured essay has three parts: Introduction, Body, Conclusion.

Introduction:
• Hook: Grab the reader's attention (quote, question, surprising fact)
• Background: Brief context for your topic
• Thesis Statement: Your main argument — one clear, specific claim

Body Paragraphs (use PEEL structure):
• Point: State your argument
• Evidence: Quote or data that supports it
• Explanation: Analyze how the evidence supports your point
• Link: Connect back to thesis or transition to next paragraph

Conclusion:
• Restate thesis (in different words)
• Summarize key points
• Closing thought: Broader significance or call to action

Transition Words:
• Adding: Furthermore, Moreover, In addition
• Contrasting: However, Nevertheless, On the other hand
• Concluding: Therefore, Thus, In conclusion, As a result

Literary devices are tools writers use to create effect and meaning.

Figurative Language:
• Simile: Comparison using 'like' or 'as'
  'Her smile was like sunshine.'
• Metaphor: Direct comparison without 'like/as'
  'He is a lion in battle.'
• Personification: Giving human traits to non-human things
  'The wind whispered through the trees.'
• Hyperbole: Exaggeration for effect
  'I've told you a million times!'
• Irony: Saying the opposite of what is meant

Sound Devices:
• Alliteration: Repetition of initial consonant sounds ('Peter Piper picked')
• Onomatopoeia: Words that sound like what they describe (buzz, crash, sizzle)
• Assonance: Repetition of vowel sounds

Structural Devices:
• Foreshadowing: Hints about future events
• Flashback: Interrupts narrative to show past events
• Symbolism: Object represents abstract idea (dove = peace)

Mastering complex grammar structures elevates writing quality.

Verb Tenses:
• Simple: I walk / I walked / I will walk
• Continuous: I am walking / I was walking
• Perfect: I have walked / I had walked / I will have walked
• Perfect Continuous: I have been walking

Subjunctive Mood (wishes, hypotheticals, demands):
• 'If I were you...' (NOT 'was')
• 'I suggest that he be present.'
• 'She demanded that it be done immediately.'

Passive Voice:
Active: 'The chef cooked the meal.'
Passive: 'The meal was cooked by the chef.'
Use passive when the action is more important than the actor.

Dangling Modifiers (common mistake):
Wrong: 'Running to school, the bell rang.'
Right: 'Running to school, I heard the bell ring.'
The modifier must clearly refer to the subject.

3.title: Advanced English
3.description: Critical analysis, rhetoric, and academic writing

chunks.content:
Literary analysis examines how a text creates meaning.

Lenses for Analysis:
• Feminist: How are gender and power represented?
• Marxist: How does class and economic power shape the narrative?
• Psychoanalytic: What do characters' motivations reveal about the unconscious?
• Post-colonial: How does the text relate to colonial power structures?

Analyzing Character:
• Protagonist vs Antagonist
• Static (unchanged) vs Dynamic (changed by events)
• Round (complex) vs Flat (one-dimensional)
• Foil: Character who contrasts the protagonist to highlight traits

Thematic Analysis:
Theme ≠ Topic. Topic = War. Theme = 'War destroys the humanity of all involved.'

How to Write Analysis:
• Make a claim (interpretation)
• Ground it in textual evidence (quotation)
• Analyze HOW the technique creates meaning — not just WHAT it says
• Connect to broader themes or context

Rhetoric is the art of persuasion. Aristotle identified three modes.

Aristotle's Appeals:
• Ethos (Credibility): 'As a doctor with 20 years experience...'
• Pathos (Emotion): Stories, vivid imagery, emotionally charged language
• Logos (Logic): Statistics, facts, logical reasoning

Common Logical Fallacies (flawed arguments):
• Ad Hominem: Attacking the person, not the argument
• Straw Man: Misrepresenting opponent's argument to attack it
• False Dichotomy: Presenting only two options when more exist
• Slippery Slope: Assuming one event will lead to extreme consequences
• Appeal to Authority: Using irrelevant authority as evidence
• Bandwagon: 'Everyone believes this, so it must be true'

Argument Structure:
Claim → Grounds (evidence) → Warrant (why evidence supports claim) → Rebuttal (addressing counterarguments)

Academic writing demands precision, evidence, and formal register.

Citation Styles:
• MLA: Author-page (Smith 45). Works Cited at end.
• APA: Author-date (Smith, 2019, p. 45). References at end.
• Chicago: Footnotes or author-date system.

Avoiding Plagiarism:
• Always cite sources — even for paraphrasing
• Quotation: Copy exact words in quotation marks
• Paraphrase: Restate in your own words (still cite!)
• Summary: Brief overview of main points (still cite!)

Academic Register:
• Avoid contractions (don't → do not)
• Avoid informal language (lots of → numerous)
• Use precise vocabulary (good → beneficial/advantageous)
• Third-person perspective generally preferred
• Hedging language: 'suggests,' 'may indicate,' 'appears to'

Research Process:
Question → Hypothesis → Literature Review → Methodology → Analysis → Conclusion
